I'm looking for an aviation, aerospace supply-chain, or China industrial-policy expert for a 30-45 minute recorded interview for my YouTube channel. The video is a documentary-style deep dive into the Comac C919, working angle: Why China Built The World's Most American Airliner. The C919 is China's answer to Boeing and Airbus. It took seventeen years and tens of billions of dollars, and it is meant to end China's dependence on Western aircraft. Yet the engines are CFM LEAP-1C from GE and Safran, and the avionics, flight controls, landing gear, APU and most major systems come from American and European suppliers. When US engine export approvals paused in 2025, the production line stalled. China built an airframe and bought almost everything else from the companies it is trying to replace. The video is not a "Boeing killer" story or a "copy that can't fly without Western permission" story. It's about why China accepted that dependence, what the C919 is actually for, and whether a fully Chinese version is realistic within a decade. I'd like someone who can explain: Why Comac chose Western suppliers rather than domestic ones, and whether it had a choice What the C919 actually is: how much is Chinese by value, and which systems matter most The CJ-1000A engine programme and how far it realistically is from certification How the 2025 export-licence pause affected production, and what it revealed about leverage What the C919 is really for: domestic market capture, industrial learning, bargaining power with Boeing and Airbus, or all three Why China's domestic airlines are ordering it, and on what terms Whether EASA or FAA certification is achievable, and whether it matters How this compares with Japan's failed SpaceJet and Russia's MC-21 What a "fully Chinese" C919 would take, and by when Whether Boeing and Airbus should be worried, and on what timescale Ideal sources: aerospace analysts, aircraft supply-chain specialists, engine industry experts, former Boeing, Airbus, GE, Safran or Comac-supplier staff, China industrial-policy academics, and journalists who have covered Comac closely. The interview takes 30-45 minutes over Zoom or similar, recorded and used in a long-form aviation/travel/business documentary with full name/title/company attribution. Reporting a feature for Deel Works. Most benefits and eligibility architecture was designed when 65 was a real exit date, and that assumption is still sitting inside plan documents. When someone doesn't leave, the rules produce consequences nobody planned for, usually one employee at a time, months after the cost lands. I need people who administer benefits inside a company. If you can't tell me your own eligibility hours threshold off the top of your head, you're not who I'm looking for. Not looking for: benefits brokers, consultants, PEO or benefits administration vendors, financial planners, retirement advisors, Medicare insurance agents, or anyone answering from the individual employee's planning side. PR representatives, please don't pitch clients whose companies sell benefits services. The hours threshold What is your benefits eligibility threshold in hours per week? When an employee reduced hours ahead of retirement, what happened to their coverage and retirement contributions? Did you carve out an exception, reclassify them, or let eligibility lapse? Have you ever declined an hours reduction because of what it would do to eligibility? What did you tell the employee? This is the one I most want to hear about. Who made that call — HR, finance, legal, the manager? Documented policy or one-off? Beyond health coverage, what else does someone lose when they drop below your threshold — retirement match, PTO accrual, life insurance, something else? Which causes the most trouble in practice? Job structure and pay Has your company changed a job description, title, or comp band to accommodate someone winding down? What was the constraint, and who had to approve it? Have you had someone stay in a role past the point where the job description still described what they did? What happened? HSA and Medicare Has an employee kept contributing to an HSA after becoming Medicare-eligible, or been caught by the six-month retroactive Part A rule? What happened, who noticed, and what did it cost them to unwind? Was it caught at enrollment, at payroll, or at tax filing? How far downstream matters to me. What do you send employees approaching 65, and at what age? If it's nothing beyond the summary plan description, please say so — that's a finding, not an embarrassment. Elder care Have you proposed an elder care benefit — referral, subsidy, backup care? What was the response and the reasoning? If turned down, what was the specific objection?
